question: It can reasonably be inferred from the passage that the second kitchen chair was moved to the landing because:

options.A: Lena's mother had cleared it out of the apartment so that Lena would have somewhere to leave her things when she arrived each morning.
options.B: the grandfather had moved into the apartment only in March and had not yet finished arranging it.
options.C: the grandfather did not want a daily reminder of his recently deceased wife.
options.D: the grandfather, no longer trusting his footing on the stairs, kept a chair on the landing where he could rest on the way up.

question: The main purpose of Passage B is to:

options.A: argue that the evidence credited to the fine-free policy is weaker than its advocates claim.
options.B: suggest that the rise in registrations was produced by digital lending and school drives rather than by any change in fine policy.
options.C: urge the library to redirect the effort spent on the fine policy toward extending hours and bus access in its poorest neighborhoods.
options.D: concede that daily fines should be dropped while arguing that the replacement charge does more harm to low-income patrons.

question: The passage identifies all of the following as contributing to the porch's decline EXCEPT:

options.A: postwar builders' tight budgets and fast schedules.
options.C: the transformation of the street into a place people drove through.
options.D: a new focal point in the interior that demanded darkness.

question: It can reasonably be inferred from the passage that a field biologist who recorded hatchlings emerging 65 days after a clutch was laid would most likely conclude that the nest had:

options.A: produced hatchlings that were mostly male.
options.B: been held near the pivotal temperature.
options.C: been laid later in the season than the nests that emerged sooner.
options.D: been laid at a warmer site than a nest that emerged after 50 days.

question: The attitude of the author of Passage B toward "a story jazz tells about itself" is best described as:

options.A: impatient with its persistence among listeners and worried mainly about its effect on how critics write.
options.B: willing to grant its truth for the greatest players while denying it to students.
options.C: skeptical of its truth and concerned about its effects.
options.D: charmed by it as a listener and resigned to its persistence among players.

question: The author's treatment of the disagreement between skeptics and advocates in the final paragraph can best be described as:

options.A: inclined toward the advocates, since the author frames the stores as infrastructure first.
options.B: even-handed, though noting that the electrification analogy rests on disputed figures.
options.C: inclined toward the skeptics, since the author grants that the stores fail as businesses.
options.D: even-handed, presenting the two sides as disagreeing about values rather than about facts.

question: As it is used in the phrase "moderates temperature swings" in paragraph 4, the word moderates most nearly means:
Which of the following best describes how defenders of automatic enrollment answer the critics described in paragraph 8?

options.A: They argue that campaigns and incentives steer people too, so the objection proves too much.
options.B: They argue that the choice stays with the employee, who is merely spared the effort of it.
options.C: They argue that some default always exists, so the only real question is which one is chosen.
options.D: They argue that so large a participation gap can only reflect what employees really wanted.

question: The main function of the fourth paragraph (beginning "Not everyone approved") is to:

options.A: trace how the trade journals' complaints changed once the studios began distributing scores.
options.B: explain why palace orchestras were better regarded by critics than neighborhood pianists.
options.C: illustrate, through the funeral foxtrot, the improvisational range the third paragraph has just described.
options.D: present the criticisms of improvised accompaniment that led studios to distribute composed scores.

question: According to the passage, Walter replaced the bell above the door because:

options.A: he wanted one thing in the shop that sounded in tune.
options.B: the mounting screws of the old one had tarnished until it could no longer be hung securely.
options.C: a visiting customer had remarked on its flat sound.
options.D: the old one had cracked and sounded worse each year.

question: The author includes the point that torpor "is not free" primarily in order to:

options.A: suggest that the table's energy savings overstate the benefit once rewarming is counted.
options.B: explain why the prevalence of deep torpor is itself evidence about which nightly danger was greater.
options.C: argue that the Andean species are common because nocturnal predators are scarce at altitude.
options.D: qualify the account of rewarming by noting that a bird which cools too far may not manage it.

question: In the final paragraph of Passage B, the narrator's attitude toward the juice bar that replaced his laundromat can best be described as:

options.A: regretful about what the neighborhood lost, though unwilling to call the change worse.
options.B: accepting on the whole, since the people on their phones seem as content as his regulars.
options.C: resigned to the sale but doubtful that a room where no one waits will keep its trade.
options.D: regretful chiefly that the lease left him no way to stay, though he grants it is brighter.
